parts.title: Part 2 · Onboarding
parts.subtitle: Find, invite and grow employer partners

steps.title: Why does work-based learning matter?
steps.takeaway: Most students find careers through people they know. WBL gives every student access to those people, not just the well-connected ones.
steps.example: At a school like yours, a junior who'd never met a nurse shadowed one for a morning. Two months later she enrolled in the CNA program at the community college.
steps.toolBlurb: Pick what matters most for your students. We'll draft a short statement you'll reuse in every outreach message.

steps.title: What challenges do employers face, and why might they resist?
steps.takeaway: Employers rarely say no because they don't care. They say no because of time, risk, or not knowing what you're asking for.
steps.example: A shop owner said “we can't take interns” and meant “I can't spare a mechanic for three months.” A one-hour career fair table was an easy yes.
steps.toolBlurb: Pick an employer type and see what's likely on their mind. Edit it to fit the businesses near you.

steps.title: What does it take to win over and keep an employer?
steps.takeaway: Employers stay when the experience is easy, personal and meaningful: one contact, small asks, quick thanks and visible impact.
steps.example: A credit union manager came back for a third year. Her reason: “Ms. Shah always sends me what the kids said afterward. That's why I keep doing it.”
steps.toolBlurb: Rate how your school does today. You'll get a score and the three changes that will matter most.

steps.title: What is the lifecycle of a school–employer relationship?
steps.takeaway: Relationships move in stages. Your job at each stage is to make the next small step obvious and easy.
steps.example: Peak Robotics started with a guest talk, then hosted a tour, then mentored the robotics team. Four years later, they take two interns every fall.
steps.toolBlurb: Click each stage to see the goal, how long it usually takes, the signals that it's time to move on, and what happens if things stall.

steps.title: Map your network and find employer partners
steps.takeaway: Your first ten partners are probably already in your building's network: staff, parents, alumni and the places students work.
steps.example: In one 20-minute staff meeting, Lincoln High's teachers listed 41 businesses they had a personal connection to.
steps.toolBlurb: Add who you know, collect leads from students, and explore local employers by industry.

steps.title: How to reach out
steps.takeaway: Personal, short and specific beats polished. Make one small ask and make it easy to say yes.
steps.example: “Hi Maria, it's Dana from Lincoln High (I'm the one who orders the oat latte!). Would you spend an hour at our career fair on Oct 15?”
steps.toolBlurb: Pick a lead, a channel and a template. We'll draft a personal message and create their invite link.

steps.title: Handling common objections
steps.takeaway: Listen first, then shrink the ask. Most objections are about time, risk or uncertainty, and each has a smaller yes.
steps.example: “We don't have time” turned into a 30-minute virtual Q&A from the owner's desk, and a worksite tour the next semester.
steps.toolBlurb: Pick what you heard. See a suggested reply, a smaller ask, and a proof point.

steps.title: Suggested first engagements
steps.takeaway: Start with a Level 1 conversation or a Level 2 school visit that fits the employer's time and comfort. A great first experience is what earns the next ask.
steps.example: Tom at Front Range Auto first chatted with Mr. Patel about what the auto tech class should cover (Level 1), then brought a diagnostic scanner to the career fair (Level 2). He's already asking about hosting a shop visit.
steps.toolBlurb: Answer three questions about an employer to get a recommended Level 1–2 activity, then plan it.

steps.title: Grow the relationship and connect employers with students
steps.takeaway: Small, warm, regular touchpoints keep partners. Student voices are the most powerful thank-you you have.
steps.example: A clinic director pinned six student thank-you notes in her break room. Her staff asked to host the next job shadow.
steps.toolBlurb: See who needs a touchpoint today, collect student thank-yous, and plan well-prepared student introductions.

steps.title: Turn relationships into WBL opportunities
steps.takeaway: When an employer is asking “what's next?”, they're ready. Propose one specific opportunity and handle the paperwork for them.
steps.example: After two great job shadow days, Lakewood Family Health asked how to host a summer intern. Ms. Gómez brought a one-page draft to the next meeting.
steps.toolBlurb: Draft a Level 3–5 opportunity (hosting, project or formal placement), then track the Colorado paperwork for that level.
